Putin warns West not to escalate, claims concerns about Russia's Kaliningrad region
If attacked, Putin says Russia willing to deploy 'all the weapons at our country's disposal'

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.

Putin, who has said Russia had no choice but to launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to safeguard its security, said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.

But he reiterated that Moscow would resort to all weapons in its arsenal, including nuclear ones, if its most westernmost territory — Kaliningrad, wedged between Poland and Lithuania — were threatened.

"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well — the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country's disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," Putin told the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow.
Putin said Russia realized it would be facing "an enemy (NATO) twice our size."

"And we will have to make use of our competitive advantages in this struggle. Yes, of course, France and Britain are nuclear powers — we understand that perfectly well and are fully aware of it," he said. "But no one else possesses the kind of weapons that Russia has today. That is our competitive advantage."

Putin's comments followed a diplomatic note that NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance Moscow would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia's Baltic exclave.

Russia's warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern over what it has portrayed as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory slightly larger than the U.S. state of Connecticut. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance responded by emphasizing that it is defensive alliance and that nuclear threats are not helpful.

Relations, already dire since Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine in 2022, have worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies those allegations and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is preparing for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios.

"We must realize that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return," he said.

"At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world's leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state," Putin said.
"Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome."

Putin, who said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump if a proper agenda were worked out first, ruled out stopping Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea region. He also acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries across Russia had cost the country one per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said Russia was now responding to Ukraine in kind.

But while he portrayed Western assistance to Kyiv in launching deep strikes inside Russia as a future threat, he said Moscow was not planning to attack European arms factories supplying Ukraine "tomorrow."
What happened in Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike and what comes next?
It remains unclear why execution failed after observers say Pike was given two doses of lethal injections
Christa Pike was to be the first woman executed in the U.S. state of Tennessee in 200 years.

But the 50-year-old, who was convicted of killing a classmate at age 18, survived two doses of lethal injections after what media observers and experts say was a "very rare" and "unprecedented" failed execution on Wednesday.
Pike's case had drawn widespread national attention as her lawyers and supporters tried to secure a stay of execution, citing her age at the time of the crime and a history of severe childhood abuse.
Her execution was delayed by several hours after a U.S. appeals court ordered a stay pending a legal review of Pike's abuse claims, but the Supreme Court ultimately ruled it could proceed.
- After day of delays, witnesses say Tennessee unable to carry out execution of Christa Pike
- Tennessee governor orders outside review after death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt

Austin Sarat, a professor at Amherst College in Massachusetts and an expert on the death penalty, said about eight per cent of lethal injections in the U.S. have been "botched," meaning something went wrong during the procedure, but the person nevertheless died.
But "what happened to Christa Pike was not a botched execution; it was a failed execution, and it's very rare," Sarat told CBC News in an interview Thursday.
"In Pike's case, insofar as we know it, the pentobarbital — the lethal drugs — had started to flow and had reached her body. That puts us in uncharted territory."
Here's what we know about what happened and what comes next.
The southern U.S. state administers pentobarbital, a barbiturate, in lethal injections.

According to the Tennessee Department of Correction's lethal injection protocol, in effect since last year and shared online by the non-profit Death Penalty Information Center, the state administers 100 millilitres of pentobarbital (for a total of 5 grams).
"If the inmate is not deceased" after that, then a second dose is given to the person, the protocol states. There is nothing in the protocol about what to do if the second lethal dose fails.
The execution had been scheduled for 10 a.m. local time Wednesday but was delayed until the evening due to legal appeals.

Catherine Sweeney, a health reporter at WPLN News, said Wednesday that Pike had been given two separate rounds of pentobarbital but was still breathing when she and the other media witnesses were told to leave.

"It was very ragged. She lifted her head up and was looking around at one point. She said that there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal," Sweeney said during a news conference.
"None of it was normal," she added. "I covered all the executions last year and most of the ones this year. We haven't seen anything like it. It went really poorly."
Another media witness, Tori Gessner of Nashville's WKRN, gave a timeline of events:
- 6:41 p.m.: Members of the media go into a separate room to witness the execution.
- 7:26 p.m.: Curtains open and Pike says her "last words."
- 7:34 p.m.: Pike says "my arm feels like it's about to burst open." Her spiritual adviser is with her. She's talking and starts "breathing, moaning, snoring."
- 7:46 p.m.: Curtains close; media witnesses can still hear Pike "breathing and snoring."
- 7:49 p.m.: Curtains reopen; "She's snoring very loudly at that point."
- 8:05 p.m.: Curtains close again; "We could still hear her audibly snoring."
- 8:53 p.m.: The microphone is cut off and media witnesses are escorted out of the room.
"Nothing about today was normal, typical — at all," Gessner told reporters.

Corinna Lain, chair of law at the University of Richmond in Virginia who has written extensively about lethal injection in the U.S., outlined three possibilities: The drug may have been degraded; the IV may have come out of Pike's vein, sending the injection into her bodily tissue; or Pike's body simply may not have reacted as expected.
But Lain stressed that "we don't know" for sure, and "that's part of the problem."
"This entire thing is covered in secrecy and it's quite perverse that the state at its most powerful moment — at the apex of its power — is killing people under a veil of secrecy," she told CBC News.
In a news release late Wednesday, the Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed the state's execution protocol.

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility."
Asked for more information about why the execution failed and on Pike's current condition, the department told CBC News in an email that it had no further comment beyond its earlier statement.
One of Pike's lawyers, Randy Spivey, told reporters on Thursday that she was alive and receiving "life-saving medical care." But he said her exact condition remained unknown.
"We at this point do not know the ramifications of the chemical torture that she has endured," he said. Her lawyers called for Pike's death sentence to be commuted.
Will Tennessee try to execute Pike again?
That also remains unclear, but Lain said the state can try again, as per a 1947 U.S. Supreme Court decision issued after an inmate survived his execution by electric chair.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Wednesday said he ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review" of Pike's execution. "Therefore, the remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year," he said in a statement, as reported by AP.
A spokesperson for the governor did not immediately respond to CBC News' emailed questions about whether the state would try to execute Pike again, and if so, when.
In May, Lee granted a one-year reprieve to another death row inmate, Tony Von Carruthers, after his execution was called off when officers failed to find a vein to administer the lethal injection.
But Sarat at Amherst College said while Pike's case raises a legal issue, it also involves a "simple matter of human decency."

"The government when it kills, or tries to kill, has an obligation to get it right. If it fails, it doesn't get another chance," he said. "One bite at the apple. That should be the norm, and Christa Pike should never have to face this horror again."
Bluebottles up to three times the usual size are washing ashore on the Gold Coast.
Scientists say little is known about the larger species' venom potency.
Lifeguards have reported relatively few stings: 20 across 39 patrolled beaches during the school holidays.
Bluebottles up to three times larger than those typically seen in Queensland waters are washing ashore on the Gold Coast, but scientists say little is known about the potency of their venom.
Griffith University marine ecologist Kylie Pitt said Physalia megalista was one of the biggest of five bluebottle species found in Australian waters.
"It doesn't turn up on the Gold Coast beaches all that often. They're usually further south," she said.
"But we don't have a lot of data about when and where they turn up."
Professor Pitt estimated the species' float or sail, which sits on the water's surface, was about 10 centimetres in length, while its stinger could stretch several metres.
"It is quite likely that the different species have got slightly different venom," she said.
"In terms of the way people react, it is dependent on the dose they get and the dose depends on the amount of tentacle that's attached to the skin."
Gold Coast City Council lifeguard supervisor Scott Franzmann said despite the busy school holidays, the impact had been relatively minor, with 20 stings reported across 39 patrolled beaches.
"It's a little bit early for bluebottles at this stage," he said.
"We don't get them until about December, January, around that Christmas period."
Gold Coast resident Tera Jesperson said she saw bluebottles the size of a fist "all over the shoreline".
"It's quite scary because our dog was going up and sniffing them," she said.
"I don't want to be stung — I never have and never want to be."
The Australian Marine Stinger Advisory Service describes bluebottle stings as "instant and sharp" but not life-threatening.
The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners recommends removing any tentacles off the skin with gloves or tweezers before washing the sting with seawater.

Professor Pitt said researchers only concluded last year that five different bluebottle species existed, with the survival of larger stingers potentially assisted by warmer El Niño conditions this season.
"The sail of the bluebottle can be offset either to the left or the right of the body's axis," she said.
"It's like having a yacht sailing on two different tacks — you'll get some more commonly deposited on beaches under north-easterlies or some more commonly deposited under north-westerlies."
Gold Coast resident Mark Wallace said he had seen similar large bluebottles further south when he was a beach inspector at Manly, Sydney.
"We could always tell when they'd come in because you'd hear a scream," he said.
"I don't know what the phenomenon is, but there must be something."

There's a new fungus amongus, and it's raising red flags among health care experts because it resists all the major antifungal treatments.
The discovery involves Candidozyma auris (formerly known as Candida auris), an emerging fungal pathogen that has already become a serious problem in hospitals around the world.

Since it was first described in 2009, this fungus has spread to more than 60 countries across six continents, causing healthcare-associated outbreaks and invasive infections, with mortality rates of 30–50 percent reported in some situations.

The fungus can persist in healthcare environments and spread easily between patients. Because of its combination of antifungal resistance and potential for wider spread, the World Health Organization designated C. auris a critical-priority fungal pathogen in 2022.
But the particular strain of this fungus described in a new paper has something especially troubling going for it: laboratory testing found it resistant to all four major classes of antifungal drugs.

The isolate was recovered from a 28-year-old woman who developed a hospital-acquired surgical-site infection after elective surgery at a hospital in Nairobi, Kenya. It's the first such case in Africa.
The woman's wound swab eventually grew C. auris, and genomic testing confirmed that the fungus belonged to one of the clades associated with high levels of antifungal resistance.

The researchers call this particular strain pan-drug-resistant, or PDR–meaning it was resistant to the antifungals in familiar drugs like fluconazole, caspofungin, micafungin, amphotericin B, and flucytosine.

Pan-drug resistance like this is exceptionally rare. The researchers describe their Kenyan isolate as the first PDR C. auris identified in Africa and only the second globally documented case; another had previously been reported in New York in 2022.
To better understand this resistance, the team sequenced its entire genome.

They found several mutations already associated with antifungal resistance, including changes in the genes ERG11 and CDR1, which are linked to resistance to azole drugs, an alteration in the FKS1 gene associated with resistance to echinocandins, and a "stop-gain" mutation in FUR1, a gene involved in processing the drug flucytosine.
The strain's genetic profile may provide clues about how its resistance arose.

The researchers note that the mutations differ from those found in previously reported strains in New York, raising the possibility that pan-drug resistance evolved independently rather than simply being imported from the United States to Kenya.

Nor can they determine whether the patient's previous exposure to antifungal drugs helped select for resistance. Her clinical history shows that she received several antifungal medications during her illness, but the researchers didn't have enough information about doses and treatment durations to establish whether those drugs drove the evolution of resistance in this particular infection.
The authors call this finding alarming, especially in regions where access to newer antifungal drugs can be limited.

The authors point to the "escalating threat of untreatable fungal infections" and call for stronger surveillance of fungal genomes, as well as "rapid diagnostic capacity to mitigate the spread of highly resistant C. auris lineages in healthcare settings," as they write in the paper.
For now, the highly resistant C. auris is super-rare. But it has already demonstrated its ability to move through hospitals, acquire resistance, and evolve in response to treatment.
A fungus that can survive nearly every standard antifungal weapon is a reminder that, in the microbial arms race, the enemy doesn't have to be common to be consequential.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports.
Update Oct. 1, 12:21 a.m. EDT (0421 UTC): SpaceX landed its two side boosters.
A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket launched from Florida Thursday night on a classified mission for the National Reconnaissance Office, America’s spy satellite agency.

Codenamed NROL-97, the mission blasted off from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 11:54 p.m. EDT (0354 UTC). It took a north-easterly trajectory on departure from Florida’s Space Coast.

The NRO has previously flown payloads on 22 Falcon 9 rockets but this is the first time it has used the heavy-lift Falcon Heavy, which consists of three Falcon 9 boosters and an upper stage, topped by a payload fairing.
The powerful rocket, which lifts off under the power of 27 Merlin 1D engines, was introduced to great fanfare in 2018 and made its 14th flight Thursday night.

Like most NRO missions, little is publicly known about the nature the flight. It was the first NRO mission to fly after being procured in 2025 through the competitive National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 3 Lane 2 contract.

The Falcon Heavy core stage, serial number B1106, was brand new and was expended on this mission. The rocket’s side boosters both flew just a month ago to launch NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. B1104 made its second flight and B1072 was on its fourth mission.

The side boosters returned to Landing Zones 1 and 2 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station with thunderous sonic booms. SpaceX returned LZ-1 to service for this mission after it was replaced by LZ-40 at Space Launch Complex 40. However, that landing pad was used earlier in the day on Thursday by the booster returning from launching the Crew 13 mission, B1101.
The NRO said the payload fairing was previously used on the NROL-95 mission in July.

If you see only one movie this year about a super-geek task force of scientists, academics, lawyers, activists, and bureaucrats who meet in a hotel conference room in St. Petersburg, Florida, in 1980 to hash out a manifesto about climate change, make that movie “A Statement” (at least, until a better one comes along). The conference I described really did take place. It was a mission dreamed up by the U.S. Congress. The issue of global warming was on the map, and the committee, gathering in Florida over a weekend for three days of meetings, was asked to devise a mission statement that would assess the dangers of climate change and make recommendations to Congress as to what, exactly, should be done about it.

“A Statement” was directed and co-written by Tom McCarthy, the sturdy carpenter of “Spotlight” and “Stillwater,” and it features some fine actors, like Paul Rudd, who plays the very diplomatic conference moderator, and Paul Giamatti, who plays a spiky Department of Energy official, and John Turturro, disarmingly elegant and funny as a professor of nuclear science at M.I.T., and Amy Ryan, as the quiet functionary who ultimately emerges as the conscience of the group.

The movie, as you’ve likely gathered, is not a tale of high-speed helicopter chases and daredevil heists. The conference — 20 men and women pontificating, arguing, strategizing, hashing out the truth — is the entire movie. “A Statement” is a film about conversation, so let me put my own prejudice forward: I’m utterly in favor of movies about conversation — humanistic legal showdowns like “12 Angry Men” (one of the greatest movies ever made), or a dinner-table dialogue like “My Dinner with Andre,” or “Before Sunrise” and its sequels, or the films of Eric Rohmer. I’m someone who actually thinks that talk is action (just ask any of my friends). And I love hearing issues argued over intelligently, which makes me the target audience for a movie like “A Statement.”

That said, I watched the film with seriously divided feelings. On paper, “A Statement” sounds like an interesting movie, but it’s at once talky and flat, grabby and meandering, impassioned and neutral. It wants to be a “firebrand” docudrama, yet I can’t imagine who the audience is going to be for it. My heartless prediction: next to no one. Not because the film is bad, but because it’s like an endless magazine article in movie form.

McCarthy and his co-screenwriters, Thomas Bidegain and Noé Debré, decided not to “dramatize” the conference. Instead, they dug the dialogue right out of the actual transcripts, presenting the conversations verbatim, which is on some level a daring choice. And McCarthy is certainly a skilled enough filmmaker to get the effect he was going for. In “A Statement,” he catches the sound and rhythm, the verbal wheel-spinning, the fuddy-duddy quibbling essence of that thing known as a strategic planning meeting.

For anyone, in any profession, who has attended such a meeting (i.e., just about anyone who has ever worked for a corporation or the government or a school system, or anyone who’s ever belonged to a guild or a union), that achievement may come off as a mixed blessing. Because the not-so-dirty secret of this kind of meeting is that while it can, at its best, get things done, the truth is that sitting there and listening to the endless jawboning and jockeying for position, the heel-digging stands followed by wilting compromise, the testy yet somehow bland infighting — all of it can be enough to make you want to curl up into a ball. In “A Statement,” what we’re really watching is the quintessence of a certain kind of middle-class American entropy.

To be fair, the mild fascination of “A Statement” is that we’re eavesdropping on 1980, seeing what people said and thought about climate change in that very different era. You might expect it all to sound well behind the curve. But the disquieting surprise of “A Statement” is that there’s no “Ah, if only they knew then what we know now!” factor. The movie is based, in part, on “Losing Earth: The Decade We Could Have Stopped Climate Change,” Nathaniel Rich’s 2019 book about the 1980s, and the central thesis of the book is that we knew it all then — or, at least, the most knowledgeable people did.

Early on, the Turturro character, Dr. David Rose, uses an overhead projector to present five slides that he’s prepared. They display graphs that chart where the carbon dioxide levels are heading and project what the damage to the environment will be. The facts are all clear (even though there’s some minor quarreling about them): the threats to the ozone layer, the primal danger of fossil fuels, the timetable of where it’s all heading.

Most of us didn’t start hearing about global warming until much later in the decade (Bill McKibben’s game-changing New York Review of Books article “Is the World Getting Hotter?” appeared in 1988), and the idea that a disparate collective like this one was fully onto it is news. So what are the people in the room arguing about? I actually wish they argued more. There’s a lot of hair-splitting, and given that the very nature of climate change is that it requires speculation, there’s a fundamental disagreement about how they should conceptualize the threat to the future. Should they say “Here’s what’s going to happen” or “Here’s what could happen”? (That’s a worthy conversation.) There are committee members who are protecting their turf, not wanting to offend the powers that be. (They include Jason Clarke as a colorfully corrupt blowhard.) But part of what we pick up on is that when it comes to the actual ideas, the voices on display aren’t really so far apart.

The two most colorful characters are Turturro’s puckish professor and Rafe Pomerance, who’s the president of Friends of the Earth. Pomerance was one of the first environmental activists to speak out on climate change, and Evan Peters, in a beard and longish hair, plays him as a fuming establishment hippie, all hyped up on everything he knows. During the meeting, he bides his time before speaking his mind, but his attitude is that the time for delaying is already gone — that the committee should advise Congress as boldly as possible.

It’s clear, at least to most of us, that he’s right: They should be sounding the alarm. Let Congress know how dire the situation is (or will be, if there’s a failure to act). But even if the committee members succeed in doing that (spoiler alert: they don’t), here’s a question: How should they advise Congress to take action? What, eactly, should be done?

Early on, there’s a moment that foreshadows what the real debate is (or should be). When Rafe, the token counterculture tree-hugger, is first introduced to the professor and learns that he’s a nuclear scientist, he makes a joke about calling him the “Big Bad Wolf.” The professor laughs it off. This is back in the era when the simple use of the word “nuclear” could make it sound like a dirty word. But, in fact, the professor is the one who truly understands what’s going on. Decades ahead of his time, he makes the point that renewables — at the time, principally solar energy — aren’t going to cut it. There’s no way that they can begin to replace fossil fuels. And guess what? They still can’t. If you want to stand up to the oil industry, only one source of energy that exists today has the potential to get us off fossil fuels, and that’s nuclear energy. And the professor comes right out and says it. (Don’t believe him? Watch the powerful Robert Stone documentary “Pandora’s Promise” or Oliver Stone’s “Nuclear Now.”)

But the professor is dismissed — by Rafe, and also by an officious lawyer (Tatiana Maslany) who’s allergic to the word “nuclear.” I was fascinated to see this subject come up in “A Statement.” Yet it gets dropped as quickly as it’s raised, and this raises a question: What is this movie really about? When you reach the surprise ending, the message seems to be that when it comes to climate change, we’ve become a society that’s a lot like Hamlet — able to talk, unable to act. And that’s a point well worth making.

But in a strange way, “A Statement” is an example of that very syndrome. On its modestly budgeted indie level, it’s yet another movie, like “Digger,” that seems to be about nothing so much as members of the Hollywood community signaling their concern. But if they’re really so concerned, why don’t they put aside the familiar tropes about climate change — the hand-wringing and the hectoring — and do something that’s really outside the box? “A Statement” catches a moment in time, and gives you an intriguing window into just how much was known at the time. Yet as a drama, the film is a bit like greenhouse gases. It traps you in a place that’s not bold enough to imagine solutions.
This protective enzyme could help stop fatty liver disease from getting worse

- Scientists have identified an enzyme that may act as a natural defense against the worsening of fatty liver disease, which affects an estimated 100 million Americans. The enzyme, called UBE2N, helps liver cells clear away damaged mitochondria and break down fat, potentially preventing the inflammation, scarring, and cell damage associated with the more dangerous condition MASH.

Researchers co-led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have identified an enzyme that may help protect the liver from the damage that can occur as the most common form of liver disease becomes more severe. The findings, from a preclinical study published in Nature Metabolism, could eventually support new strategies for preventing serious liver injury and progression toward liver failure.

An estimated 100 million people in the U.S. have metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, according to the American Liver Foundation. Roughly 20% to 25% of those affected go on to develop metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a more serious form of the condition in which excess liver fat is accompanied by inflammation, cell injury and scarring.

Current care mainly centers on lifestyle changes and efforts to limit additional liver damage. Although medications are available, treatment options are still limited, and there is currently no cure for MASH.

Earlier research has suggested that damaged mitochondria, the structures that produce energy for cells, may contribute to the development and progression of MASH. In the new multicenter study, Cedars-Sinai researchers found that levels of an enzyme called UBE2N decline in liver cells as the disease becomes more advanced.

"The UBE2N enzyme appears to protect the liver from the inflammation and damage associated with MASH by helping remove damaged mitochondria and supporting the breakdown of fat," said Ekihiro Seki, MD, PhD, professor of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences at Cedars-Sinai and co-corresponding author of the study. "When levels of the enzyme fell, we saw more damaged cells and injury to the liver."
Restoring UBE2N Reduced Liver Damage in Mice
The researchers then restored UBE2N to normal levels in the livers of laboratory mice. After doing so, they observed reductions in fat accumulation, inflammation and scarring.
Those results suggest that UBE2N could become a potential treatment target for preventing MASLD from advancing to MASH.

"The identification of this enzyme's role in regulating mitochondria in the liver is an important advance in understanding steatotic liver disease," said Shelly Lu, MD, the Women's Guild Chair in Gastroenterology and director of the Karsh Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at Cedars-Sinai. "Future studies can test whether enhancing this protective pathway can complement existing treatments, identify patients most likely to benefit and lead to new therapeutic approaches for preventing advanced disease."

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”
Capcom is preparing for a ‘future where we create games together with AI’
During a presentation on the future of RE Engine, Capcom laid out its plans to embrace AI in ‘development workflows.’

Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.

The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.

The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.

Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.

When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.

Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.

Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.

Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

Culver City protesters demand Sony, Amazon, other studios defend democracy
- Braving 100-degree heat, protesters marched through Culver City demanding local media corporations do their part to defend democracy.
- The “Business for Democracy Pledge” was sent to the CEOs of Sony Pictures, Apple, Pinterest and Amazon. So far none have responded.
- The march comes amid growing anxieties over the upcoming November elections.
On a sweltering Saturday, around 100 people gathered in Culver City for a rally and march to deliver a message to several major media companies: Help us protect our democracy.

Spotlighting Sony Pictures Studios, Apple, Pinterest and Amazon MGM Studios, all with local offices, protesters demanded that the companies sign on to the “Business for Democracy Pledge” ahead of the elections in November.

After hearing from a few speakers outside Culver City’s City Hall, the band of demonstrators marched a few blocks to the offices of Sony Pictures Studios. From there — walking by posters for the upcoming Sony release “The Social Reckoning” — they made their way back across downtown Culver City to stop outside the historic Culver Studios, now owned by Amazon MGM.

Local groups Culver City and Friends Rising and Keep Showing Up led the protests. This week, they sent letters to the chief executives of all four corporations asking them to sign the pledge. No response has been received. (Messages from The Times to spokespeople for all four companies also were not returned.)

“Businesses and particularly large corporations like Sony, Apple, Pinterest and Amazon, who are our focus today, have a particular role to play in defending democracy,” Phil Ansell, leader of Culver City and Friends Rising, said before the rally. “They have weight, and this administration cares what business says.”

He added, “We’ve seen internationally that in situations where democracy has been under threat, that when the business community stands up for democracy, it can make a huge difference in preventing a full-on shift to authoritarianism.”
L.A. voting rights groups rally to recruit poll watchers, launch protection programs, and counter potential election disruption in the November vote.

Bryan “Bubba” Fish, Vice-Mayor of Culver City, was on hand as a featured speaker and noted how Culver City, a relatively small community that is home to offices for multiple international media companies, is uniquely positioned to help ensure residents’ voices are heard.

“The message of this event is that these major corporations, that are the largest and richest corporations in the history of the planet, benefit from our civilized society,” Fish said before the rally. “...The only reason they’ve been able to grow to the size that they are is because we have stable, legitimate governance, and the bare minimum should be that they commit to defending and speaking out when our elections and our democracy is at risk. That should be the floor.”
Fish added, “We’re here saying you’re a part of our community, stand for free and fair elections and defend democracy alongside us.”
Reverend Dr. Frances Wattman Rosenau, pastor at Culver City Presbyterian Church, spoke outside of both Sony and Amazon MGM.

“Democracy is one of our core values as a country, and me as a person of faith, I care deeply about giving voice to the voiceless and making sure that no one is marginalized,” Rosenau said while walking from one location to the other. “And calling our business partners to come alongside us is an act of partnership. It’s time for everybody to be in the boat and rowing, affirming what we stand for as a people for the common good.”

The Culver City event is one of a series around the country this week in collaboration with the group May Day Strong. Representatives of other local activist groups, including PowerSwitch Action, National Nurses United and Singing Resistance Santa Monica, were also in attendance on Saturday.
Amy Schur, campaign director with Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment (ACCE), is involved with coordinating the national campaign for the “Business for Democracy” pledge.

“We’re in a unique moment where people are rising up all across the country of their own accord,” Schur said. “People are seeing what’s at stake. So they’re ready to march, they’re ready to speak out.”
Schur noted that much work remains to harness that energy and turn it into real change.

“The critical question is, can we do it in ways that are strategic and have the impact that we need in this moment?” she said. “Just marches are not enough because it’s kind of easy to ignore those. But when it’s a march with a purpose and calling out big corporations, it has more impact.”
Ansell noted that companies such as Apple and Amazon spoke out after the insurrection of Jan. 6, 2021 and hopes they will continue in that same spirit.

“We’re here today to say don’t wait for the equivalent of January 6 to happen again,” Ansell said. “Commit yourself now publicly to opposing any efforts to undermine this election. And our view is that to the extent that many large corporations across this country take that public stance, it will significantly reduce the risk of a major effort to subvert this election.”
Organizers see Saturday’s protest as part of an ongoing effort and hope more people will feel empowered to participate.

“People are not alone,” Ansell said. “No one should feel like they have to stay home alone and despair. There are many opportunities for action, and we have to be prepared. Today’s action is one of many to defend this election.”
